title: SYSK Selects: Sherpas: Warm, Friendly Living
summary: Chuck introduces this SYSK Selects rerun of the April 2011 episode "Sherpas: Warm Friendly Living." Josh and Chuck cover the Sherpa people: their migration from Tibet to the Solu Khumbu region of Nepal around the 16th century, farming with terraces, buckwheat and later potatoes, carrying loads by trumpline rather than wheels, and their Tibetan Buddhist culture. They discuss Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay's 1953 Everest summit, the British Everest expeditions and colonial-era Darjeeling, the Sherpa's unsung role, sherpa mountaineering and tourism, famous Sherpa climbers, women Sherpas, porters, and the yeti. The episode closes with listener mail from M about Disney theme park dirt.

entities.name: Indiana Jones and the Raiders of the Lost Ark

segments.title: Rerun introduction by Chuck
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this Selects episode, a rerun of the April 2011 Sherpas episode, and explains why the hosts wanted to highlight Sherpa people.

segments.title: Sherpa name, origins and migration
segments.summary: The hosts clarify the spelling and meaning of Sherpa as a people, a last name and an occupation. They discuss the Sherpa migration from Tibet to the Solu Khumbu region of Nepal around the 16th century, fleeing warfare, and the area being uninhabited when they arrived.

segments.title: Farming, terraces and crops
segments.summary: The Sherpas moved between higher and lower villages to adapt to altitude sickness. They grew buckwheat and wheat, then potatoes introduced in the mid-nineteenth century, and built terraced fields on steep slopes.

segments.title: Carrying loads without wheels
segments.summary: The hosts discuss that Sherpas have no wheeled vehicles or wheelbarrows and carry everything, including bundles of firewood, by trumpline, a strap around the forehead.

segments.title: Edmund Hillary and the Sherpa foundation
segments.summary: The Sherpa culture is described as isolated and without a written language until the 1960s. Sir Edmund Hillary later set up a foundation that brought schools and hospitals to the Sherpa, though schools are now in poor shape.

segments.title: Everest history, British expeditions and Sherpa recognition
segments.summary: Nepal was closed to outsiders until about 1949, and Everest was recognized as the highest peak in 1865. Darjeeling was a British hub where Sherpas were first hired for expeditions, and Alexander Kellas introduced Western climbers to Sherpas. Hillary and Tenzing Norgay summited in 1953 as part of a four-person British expedition, and they received different honors.

segments.title: Sherpa earnings, Buddhism and Everest tourism
segments.summary: Sherpas who climb and trek earn substantially more than the average Nepali. Their Tibetan Buddhist beliefs encourage helping others, and the hosts discuss tension over tourism, crowding, pollution and deforestation on Everest.

segments.title: Famous Sherpa climbers, women and porters
segments.summary: The hosts name notable Sherpa climbers, including Apa Sherpa, Babu Chiri Sherpa, Lhakpa Gelu Sherpa and Ming Kipa Sherpa, and Pemba Lambu Sherpa as the first woman. They discuss women becoming climbers and taking over household duties, and the lower-paid porters and advocacy groups.

segments.title: The yeti and Hillary's search
segments.summary: The hosts describe the yeti as a mythical Himalayan creature akin to Bigfoot. Hillary went back in 1960 to search for yetis after seeing footprints he believed were yeti tracks, but he found nothing.

segments.title: Wrap-up on Sherpas
segments.summary: The hosts close the Sherpa topic, noting dwindling population in the park and a survey on Western influence, and point to further reading.

segments.title: Listener mail: Disney dirt
segments.summary: Listener M shares Disney theme park stories from a former cast member, including a legendary table behind Pirates of the Caribbean, Jungle Cruise skipper lore, and rumors of body bags and ghost stories under Space Mountain.

segments.title: Sign-off and listener call to action
segments.summary: The hosts close with a listener prompt about state secession and mention where to find more on the HowStuffWorks site.
